summary.text: DAFT / DAFT-2 tests whether a modified TSI P-Trak particle counter works accurately in microgravity, by comparison with a DustTrak, to reduce risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment.

measurements.text: Aerosol particle counts from the modified P-Trak compared with the DustTrak CNC, using Arizona Red Dust aerosol in 15-liter Mylar bags.

hardware.text: TSI P-Trak modified with a capillary-force condenser tube and without the mercury switch; DustTrak CNC as comparison instrument.

claims.text: DAFT / DAFT-2 aims to test that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.
The investigation aims to compare the TSI P-Trak performance against the DustTrak control.
The investigation hypothesizes that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.

limitations.text: The metadata states objectives, hypotheses and approach but no measured result of the P-Trak versus DustTrak comparison.
This draft cites PSI metadata and no PDF text. The packet also includes official table passages whose findings have not been incorporated or reviewed.

modeling_resources.description: Analyzed flight data files for the P-Trak and DustTrak comparison listed in the PSI file inventory.

evidence.excerpt: DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.
Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.

TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion.
The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts.
